summary: Kole Jain walks through eight ways to present one UI design: six creative 'showcase' techniques for portfolios and social media, and two professional techniques for client meetings. The showcase techniques build up from a plain, muted background with a faint shadow (or an accent-colored glow in dark mode), to letting the design extend off the frame, skewing it, popping one element out, arranging several screens into an ungridded collage, and pairing the UI with relevant photos. For clients he argues the goal changes from impressing them to building confidence, so he recommends device mockups (including custom ones made with AI image generation and a green screen) and working prototypes that show hidden interactions such as swipe actions and modal animations. For someone building a design system, this gives a checklist for how finished components and screens should be shown to stakeholders, and a clear split between showcase shots and client-facing presentation.
key_ideas: Presentation is half of a design: the same UI looks better when it is presented well.
Creative showcase techniques suit portfolios and social media; client meetings need realistic context instead.
A plain, muted background is the safest showcase and works for nearly any design, because it lets the design itself pop.
For a light-mode design, derive the background from the accent color by darkening and desaturating it, since a bright color would compete with the design.
For a dark-mode design, large blurred circles of the accent color behind the UI create a soft ambient glow.
Letting the design or its pattern extend off the frame ('exploding the image') makes it more visually interesting than a tidy crop.
A slight skew draws attention; popping one part out with an offset and shadow draws even more.
Multiple screens look better offset, slid off the page or arranged in a collage that deliberately does not line up in a grid.
Collages need large designs such as landing pages; dashboards are better shown by zooming into one section and animating it.
Photos in a showcase need to be relevant without distracting, and are often better for physical products; for software, fluid gradient images sometimes work.
In client meetings the goal is to build confidence in the product, so mockups show the product where it will actually be used.
In the creator's view, AI is not great at making thoughtful UIs but is good at making custom mockup scenes.
Prototypes show rather than describe, and reveal hidden features such as swipe actions and animation sequences.
Small details sell the whole experience, in a mockup scene just as in UI design.

rules.rule: For a light-mode showcase, make the background from the accent color darkened and desaturated toward gray, not a bright color.
rules.why: Brighter colors would pop more than the design itself.
rules.evidence: take our orange accent color, darken it, and desaturate it

rules.rule: Add a faint shadow to the design when it sits on a plain showcase background.
rules.why: With the muted background, a faint shadow already makes it look fantastic.
rules.evidence: Add a faint little shadow

rules.rule: For a dark-mode showcase, place large blurred circles of the accent color behind the UI to create a subtle glow.
rules.why: It creates a soft ambient light that makes the design feel like it is emitting light.
rules.evidence: adding some large blurred circles of our accent color behind the UI

rules.rule: Consider a glassy background with a soft gradient stroke to define the design's edges.
rules.why: It adds another layer of depth.
rules.evidence: glassy background paired with a soft gradient stroke

rules.rule: Default to a plain, relatively bland background for showcase shots before reaching for effects.
rules.why: Relatively bland backgrounds make the design itself pop; it's tough to go wrong with this and it works for nearly any design.
rules.evidence: Don't underestimate minimalism

rules.rule: Let lines, patterns or the design itself extend off the frame instead of cropping it tightly.
rules.why: Allowing it to expand makes it much more visually interesting than cropping it down; the source admits it isn't super practical but calls it a cool effect.
rules.evidence: exploding the image

rules.rule: Don't skew the design too much, just enough to get the effect (the example uses 2° vertically and -14° horizontally).
rules.why: A skew attracts attention to the UI; the source says to use just enough to get the effect.
rules.evidence: Make sure not to skew too much

rules.rule: To draw more attention to the key element, pop it out by offsetting it and adding a shadow; optionally leave a gray placeholder where it was.
rules.why: It draws even more attention to that element; the placeholder sometimes accentuates the effect but is not always necessary.
rules.evidence: pop the dashboard out by offsetting it and adding a shadow

rules.rule: Do not stack multiple screens; offset them and slide them slightly off the page, or build a collage.
rules.why: Stacking is pretty boring and doesn't work well.
rules.evidence: Stacking them is pretty boring

rules.rule: In a multi-screen collage, avoid lining everything up in a grid; a few degrees of rotation or a skew can be added.
rules.why: A grid is not as interesting, and a few degrees of rotation adds a lot of motion.
rules.evidence: everything lines up in a grid because that's not as interesting

rules.rule: Use collages for large designs such as landing pages; for a dashboard, zoom into one section and animate it a touch instead.
rules.why: Dashboard details are too fine to really see in a collage.
rules.evidence: the design itself should be large

rules.rule: Only add photos to a showcase when they are relevant and do not distract from the UI, such as for a physical product.
rules.why: Images are the hardest to balance with the UI; they work better for physical products like a coffee shop or a car.
rules.evidence: relevant but also not distract from the design

rules.rule: In client meetings, present the design in device mockups that show where the product will be used, not in creative showcase compositions.
rules.why: The goal is to build confidence; a clear, realistic context lets the client understand what the final product will look like.
rules.evidence: the best way to immerse a client in the design is through mock-ups

rules.rule: Use the latest Apple product as the device in a custom mockup.
rules.why: The source calls it the gold standard.
rules.evidence: The gold standard is to use the latest Apple product

rules.rule: Use AI to generate custom mockup scenes (prompt for a green screen on the device, then punch out the green and skew the design in), rather than relying on it for the UI itself.
rules.why: The source does not think AI is great at making thoughtful UIs, but says it is good at making mockups.
rules.evidence: it is good at making mock-ups

rules.rule: Show a working prototype instead of describing interactions, especially hidden ones like swipe actions or animation sequences.
rules.why: It lets people feel the experience and communicates polish and thoughtfulness that static images can't.
rules.evidence: Don't describe, show

rules.rule: In a multi-screen collage, pop out one frame if it is more important than the rest, such as the hero section.
rules.why: It singles out the most important frame; the source offers it as a further option after rotation or skew.
rules.evidence: pop out one of the frames if it's more important

rules.rule: For mobile designs, offset the screens and slide them slightly off the page in the opposite orientation.
rules.why: The source says this is good and works well for mobile designs in the opposite orientation.
rules.evidence: works well for mobile designs in the opposite orientation

rules.rule: For software products shown with images, consider fluid gradient images instead of photos.
rules.why: The source says fluid gradient images sometimes work well for software, though the other showcase methods are more typical.
rules.evidence: For softwares, sometimes fluid gradient images work well

rules.rule: To take a client mockup further, use a lifestyle mockup that shows the UI actually being used on a device such as an iPad or Apple Watch.
rules.why: The source says it can really elevate the design.
rules.evidence: a lifestyle mockup where the UI is actually being used

rules.rule: Put small, specific details in a custom mockup scene prompt (for example small cracks or a water stain).
rules.why: It's the small details that sell the entire experience, just like with any UI design.
rules.evidence: Minimal concrete cylinders with small cracks

rules.rule: When designing for e-commerce, make high-quality product mockups.
rules.why: The source says high-quality product mockups are the difference between great and disastrous designs in e-commerce.
rules.evidence: useful if you're designing in e-commerce

process.detail: Decide whether the presentation is a creative showcase (portfolio, social media) or professional (client meeting).
Light mode: darken and desaturate the accent color and add a faint shadow. Dark mode: add large blurred accent-color circles for a glow, or use a glassy background with a soft gradient stroke.
Optionally let the design extend off the frame, skew it slightly (for example 2° vertical, -14° horizontal) and pop out the key element with an offset and shadow.
Offset and slide screens off the page, or build an ungridded collage with slight rotation; pop out the most important frame. For dashboards, zoom into one section and animate it.
Add photos only if they are relevant and don't distract, mainly for physical products.

process.step: Generate a custom mockup with AI
process.detail: Prompt for the latest Apple device with a green screen on its screen in a detailed scene (for example a MacBook Air on an orange faux leather padded chair, background blurred, soft shadows, moody lighting), punch out the green background, and skew the design in. Small details in the scene sell it.
Build a working prototype to show hidden features like common swipe actions, a create-link modal animating in, or the animation sequence when a link is deleted.

examples.what: Light-mode dashboard on a muted background
examples.visual_note: The orange accent is darkened and desaturated to a grayish background with a faint shadow under the UI, so the design pops more than the background.
Large blurred accent-color circles behind a dark UI create ambient light, as if the design emits it.
Relatively bland background colors that still work because the design itself stands out.
Lines from the dashboard extend down and the dashboard expands off the screen; a slider's pattern also extends off the frame.
Instead of a piece of the UI, the brand's visual identity is extended with important metrics added to it.
The dashboard is skewed 2° vertically and -14° horizontally, then offset with a shadow, sometimes with a gray placeholder where it sat.
Landing page screens are offset, slightly rotated or skewed and not aligned to a grid, with the hero section popped out.
A close-up of one dashboard section, lightly animated, reading as both creative and professional.
Photos are blended into the UI without being overbearing.
A MacBook Air with a green screen on an orange faux leather padded chair with a notebook and stool, blurred background and moody lighting; the green is replaced with the skewed design.
Minimal concrete cylinders with small cracks in a beige living room with a water stain, showing how small details sell the scene.
The UI shown in use on an iPad or on an Apple Watch screen.
A create-link modal elegantly animating in, and the animation sequence when a link is deleted, plus common swipe actions.
The design on a plain computer without much else, which already does a lot to frame it for a client.
